'''''Montia fontana''''', '''blinks''' is a herbaceous annual to perennial plant that grows in freshwater springs in upland regions, and in seasonally damp acid grassland in the lowlands. It is widespread throughout the world, except in southern Asia. It is rather variable in morphology, which is reflected in a complex history of taxonomy. Currently, there are three accepted subspecies which are defined largely by the appearance of the seedcoat. It is edible and consumed as a salad in some areas, but is otherwise of minimal economic impact. Because of its association with clean water habitats, it is often viewed as a species of conservation value.

==Description==
Blinks is an annual to perennial prostrate [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] with branching stems, sometimes forming mats up to 50 cm across in short, seasonally damp grassland or floating in streams and hollows. The stems are thin (0.5 mm diameter) and reddish, sometimes rooting in water. The primary roots are fleshy and pink, and there are numerous secondary roots with fibrous hairs.

The [[Glossary of leaf morphology|spatulate]] leaves are succulent and glabrous, arranged in opposite pairs, between 2–20 mm long and 1.5–6 mm wide, with a [[hydathode]] at the tip. On some plants, particularly those floating in water, the leaves have a distinct petiole, whereas on those (mainly subsp. ''chondrosperma'') which grow in dry grassland, the leaves narrow towards their bases and fuse with the opposite one at the stem (i.e. they are [[Connation|connate]]).
[[File:Montia fontana connate.jpg|thumb|The leaves on a small plant are often joined at the base.]]

The inflorescence consists of a terminal cyme of two or three tiny white flowers 2–3 mm in diameter with five petals, two sepals, 3-5 stamens, 1-3 styles, each with one stigma. 
The fruit capsules are 2 mm in diameter and contain 3 round seeds. The architecture of the seeds differentiates the four subspecies of blinks.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C & M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref name=Sell1>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 1 |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0-521-55335-3}}</ref><ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref><ref name="Walters" />

==Taxonomy==
The name ''Montia fontana'' was coined by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in 1753 in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', but it has had many synonyms before and since; Linnaeus lists "''Montia aquatica minor''", "''Cameraria aquatica minor''" and "''Portulaca arvensis''" among them.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linnaeus |first=C. |title=Species Plantarum |year=1753 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13829#page/99/mode/1up}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=''Montia fonatana'' L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/9004024 |access-date=10 February 2024 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref>

The generic name ''Montia'' is a tribute to [[Giuseppe Monti]] (1682-1760), a professor of botany at Bologna.<ref name=Leighton>{{cite book |last1=Leighton |first1=W.A. |title=A Flora of Shropshire |date=1841 |publisher=John van Voorst |location=London}}</ref> The epithet ''fontana'' derives from the Latin ''[[wiktionary:fontana|fontanus]]'', a spring, and refers to its habitat. The common name "blinks" may come from the Old English "[[wiktionary:blink|blincan]]", to shine or twinkle. Other common names for it include "water blinks", "water chickweed" or (in the US) "annual water miner's lettuce".

Because blinks is such a widespread and variable species, many synonyms have been coined, and many subspecies have been described which reflect this variability. The currently accepted account is largely based on that of [[Max Walters]] in the British journal ''Watsonia'' in 1953.<ref name=Walters>{{Cite journal |last=Walters |first=S.M. |date=1953 |title=Montia fontana L. |url=https://archive.org/details/wats-3p-1 |journal=Watsonia |volume=3 |pages=1–6}}</ref> In this paper he described 4 subspecies:

* subsp. ''fontana'', which has smooth, shiny seeds 1.1-1.35 mm in diameter and occurs in very wet places worldwide, often growing as a floating plant with petiolate leaves.
* subsp. ''chondrosperma'' (Fenzl) Walters, which has less shiny seeds 1.0-1.2 mm diameter and occurs on sandy soils in lowland places. It is a small plant (~1 cm tall) with connate leaf bases.
* subsp. ''intermedia'' (Beeby) Walters, which has shiny tuberculate seeds 0.85-1.1 mm diameter and grows in very wet places in Western Europe and Australia. This is now called ''Montia fontana'' subsp. ''amporitana'' Sennen.<ref name="POWO" />
* subsp. ''variabilis'' Walters, which has smooth seeds 0.9-1.1 mm diameter and grows in wet places in Britain and possibly elsewhere. This is no longer considered a valid taxon.<ref name="POWO" />
[[File:Montia fontana chondrosperma L. (AM AK362182-3).jpg|thumb|The seedcoat is important in identifying the subspecies; this is subsp. ''chondrosperma''.]]

==Distribution and status==
Blinks has an almost world-wide distribution, and it is considered a native species in most places, and in all continents except [[Antarctica]]. It is apparently considered an introduction only in [[Venezuela]] and the [[Falkland Islands]], and it is absent only from southern Asia.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Montia fontana L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/9004024 |access-date=17 February 2024 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref><ref name=POWO>{{Cite web |title=Montia fontana L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:311155-2 |access-date=17 February 2024 |website=Plants of the World Online}}</ref>

The threat status of Blinks globally and in Europe is [[Least-concern species|LC]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Blinks ''Montia fontana'' |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/164123/63307717 |access-date=14 February 2024 |website=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species}}</ref> as it is in Britain,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref> where it is common and widespread in the north and west, becoming scattered and rare towards the south and east. Despite its abundance, it is listed as an [[axiophyte]] in most British counties.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/axiophytes |access-date=14 February 2024 |website=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Montia fontana (mezenc, 43, France)2.JPG|thumb|A sward of blinks in a flush in France]]
Blinks grows in a wide range of wetland habitats, from permanently wet pools, springs and streamsides to winter-wet, sandy grassland. It mostly grows in acid places, but is tolerant of mildly alkaline conditions. Its altitudinal range in Britain is from sea level to 996 m in Coire Leachavie, [[Glen Affric]].<ref name=Schou>{{Cite book |last=Schou |first=J.C. |title=Aquatic Plants of Northern and Central Europe including Britain and Ireland |last2=Moeslund |first2=B. |last3=van de Weyer |first3=K. |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2023 |isbn=978-0-691-25101-1 |location=Princeton, N.J.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/altitudes}}</ref> The flowers are either pollinated by insects or (especially if underwater, when they are often [[Cleistogamy|cleistogamous]]) will self-pollinate.<ref name="Schou" />

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 9, R = 5, N = 3 and S = 0, which show that it occurs in fairly sunny places with slightly acid damp soils and low nutrient conditions. It is not tolerant of salt.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1-870393-48-1|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|access-date=13 February 2024}}</ref>

Under the European system for classifying habitats, [[European Environment Agency#European Nature Information System|EUNIS]], Blinks is a characteristic species in three habitats, comprising four communities: C2.18 acid oligotrophic vegetation of spring brooks; C2.25 acid oligotrophic vegetation of fast-flowing stream; and D2.2C soft water spring mires, including D2.2C11 montane soft water moss springs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Montie des fontaines |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/108785 |access-date=20 February 2024 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref> Within the [[British National Vegetation Classification|British NVC]] blinks (particularly subsp. ''fontana'') occurs in several types of upland spring-fed vegetation, most characteristically M35 ''Ranunculus omiophyllus''-''Montia fontana'' rills,<ref name=Rodwell2>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 2: Mires and heaths|year=1991 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=0-521-39165-2}}</ref> and (mainly subsp. ''chondrosperma'') in summer-dry, rain-fed U1 ''Festuca ovina-Agrostis capillaris-Rumex acetosella'' grassland in sandy, more lowland habitats.<ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref><ref name=Trueman>{{cite book |last1=Trueman |first1=I.C. |last2=Poulton |first2=M.W. |last3=Hodder |first3=M.|title=The Flora of Sutton Park |date=2023 |publisher=Pisces Publications |location=Newbury |isbn=978-1-913994-09-9}}</ref>
[[File:Montia fontana fruits.jpg|thumb|''Montia fontana'' subsp. ''chondrosperma'' in a grassy sward, already going to seed in April.]]

Blinks is occasionally found in secondary populations in other habitats, such as woodland stream sides, where it has presumably been washed up, or in bowling greens or pavements after habitats have been built over.<ref name=GGG>{{cite book |last1=Graham |first1=G.G. |title=The Flora and Vegetation of County Durham |date=1988 |publisher=Durham County Conservation Trust |isbn=0-905362-02-0}}</ref><ref name=Crawley>{{cite book |last1=Crawley |first1=M.J. |title=The Flora of Berkshire |date=2005 |publisher=Brambleby Books |location=Harpenden |isbn=0-9543347-4-4}}</ref><ref name=Trueman/>

The beetle ''[[Phaedon armoraciae]]'' chews on its leaves in Scotland,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Coleoptera >> Chrysomelidae >> Phaedon armoraciae (L.) |url=https://dbif.brc.ac.uk/interactions.aspx?insectid=6441&hostid=3476 |access-date=13 February 2024 |website=Database of Insects and their Food Plants}}</ref> and the smut-like [[ascomycete]] ''[[Tolyposporium|Tolyposporium montiae]]'' <small>(Rostrup) Rostrup, 1904</small> can infest the root collar area.<ref name=bladmineerders>{{Cite web |title=Tolyposporium montiae |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/parasites/fungi/dikarya/basidiomycota/ustilaginomycotina/ustilaginomycetes/ustilaginales/anthracoideaceae/tolyposporium/tolyposporium-montiae/ |access-date=16 February 2024 |website=Plant Parasites of Europe}}</ref> There is a species of vinegar fly, ''[[Scaptomyza|Scaptomyza graminum]]'' whose larvae produce leaf mines in blinks; it has been recorded in Britain and Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MONTIA. Blinks. [Portulacaceae] |url=https://www.ukflymines.co.uk/Keys/MONTIA.php |access-date=17 February 2024 |website=The leaf and stem mines of British flies and other insects}}</ref><ref name="bladmineerders" />

==Uses==
Blinks is edible and is gathered in the wild and used as a salad vegetable in Spain and Portugal, but it is not currently cultivated. It is high in fibre and is a rich source of omega-3 fatty acids.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tardio |first=J. |date=2011 |title=''Montia fontana'' L. (Portulacaceae), an interesting wild vegetable traditionally consumed in the Iberian Peninsula |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10722-011-9749-7 |journal=Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution |volume=58 |pages=1105–1118}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Morales |first=Patricia |title=Fatty acids profiles of some Spanish wild vegetables |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/153408952.pdf |access-date=24 February 2024}}</ref>
